126: ## 3. Not verified, and why
127: 
128: - npm's publish-time name checks beyond punctuation similarity (typosquat heuristics), and a race for a free name: only a publish shows them.
129: - Whether the maintainer owns an npm scope: `npm view @x/y` is 404 either way, `whoami` is forbidden, npmjs.com answered HTTP 403.
130: - GitHub rename redirects: cited from GitHub's docs ("Renaming a repository": web, clone, fetch and push redirect; a new repo
131:   with the old name breaks them), not tested (renaming is a write).
132: - The real global config, store, log, herdr directory and the private chezmoi store (forbidden): the exact form of the
133:   global entry, and any herdr `readonly-guard.json`.
134: - That `dist/` still works after the folder moves (the bundle has no path I know of; not checked), `npx` with a bin named
135:   differently from the package, and what an old-name stub package would do (needs a publish).
136: - A command run through two live write guards (no model); the policy-union inference in scenario A.
137: - opencode 2.x: whether V2 plugin storage is keyed by the plugin id (no 2.x installed).
138: - A clean single-pass integration run: it needed a re-run of 4 tests (see 5), the machine being loaded by other workers.
139: 
140: ## 4. Recommendation
141: 
142: **Design.** One source of truth for the names: the families are `package`, `short` (store, log dir, herdr file, message
143: prefix), `snake` (tool ids, permission), `UPPER` (env), `review command`. Rename in one change with `prototype/rename.ts`
144: (reproducible, skips `memory/`, keeps the registry keys), then add the shims below in the same PR, because the first
145: renamed build is the one the maintainer's own sessions load.
146: 
147: Shims (hand-written, small): (1) options: option > `<NEW>_STORE|DATA` > old env var > new default path > old default path
148: when only that exists; (2) the same for the herdr-dir file; (3) `doctor` accepts the old package name and the old env
149: vars, and prints the one-line `mv` that finishes the move; (4) registry keys stay `opencode-readonly-guard.copies.v1` and
150: `.failed.v1` (a comment says why); (5) CHANGELOG: "renamed from opencode-readonly-guard". Remove (1)-(3) after 1-2 releases.
151: A zero-shim variant is possible because the maintainer is the only user: two `mv` commands (store, log dir) and one edited
152: config line; then only (4) is needed. That trades safety of the first run for ~60 lines less.
153: 
154: **Plan for the best two** (identical shape; derived strings differ):
155: 
156: | Derived string | `opencode-agent-policy`                               | `opencode-clearance`                       |
157: | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
158: | short / store  | `agent-policy`, `agent-policy.json`, log `agent-policy/` | `clearance`, `clearance.json`, `clearance/` |
159: | env            | `AGENT_POLICY_STORE`, `AGENT_POLICY_DATA`             | `CLEARANCE_STORE`, `CLEARANCE_DATA`         |
160: | tools / perm.  | `agent_policy_review`, `_update`, `_allow`            | `clearance_review`, `_update`, `_allow`     |
161: | command        | `/policy-review` (script flag `--command`)            | `/clearance-review`                         |
162: 
163: Steps, in this order:
164: 
165: 1. Decide the name; re-run `names-npm.ts`, `names-similar.ts`, `names-gh.ts` that day (scripted).
166: 2. Rename PR in a worktree: `bun prototype/rename.ts --to <pkg> --command <cmd> --from-dir . --into <copy>` shows the diff
167:    first; apply in place, hand-edit README prose, `keywords` (`read-only`, `guard`), CHANGELOG, the TODO publish item;
168:    `prettier --write`; add the shims and their tests; `mise run check`. Scripted: ~90% of the text.
169: 3. `mise run test:integration` in that worktree only (the build replaces that checkout's `dist/`, see AGENTS "Hazards").
170: 4. Hosting (maintainer): `gh repo rename <new>`, then `git remote set-url origin <new url>` once (remotes live in the shared
171:    `.git/config`). Never create a repository under the old name (breaks the redirect). Nothing else points at the repo.
172: 5. Local switch in a quiet moment, never half done (scenario C): build the renamed checkout first, then either keep the
173:    folder name until the global entry is edited, or `mv [redacted:repo] ~/Work/<new>`, run `git worktree repair`
174:    for every linked worktree, `ln -s <new> <old>` (verified E/F), edit the global entry, drop the symlink later.
175:    Running sessions keep the copy they loaded.
176: 6. Update the 11 markdown files and the shell script in siblings (scripted `rg -l` + sed after review); leave transcripts.
177: 7. First publish under the new name, release workflow with provenance, trusted publisher created for the new repo.
178: 8. After 1-2 releases: remove shims; keep the registry keys.
179: 
180: **Keeping `opencode-readonly-guard` resolvable.** Before the first publish nothing on npm can point at the new name:
181: `npm deprecate` needs a published version and npm has no redirect or alias. Possible: the GitHub redirect (web, clone,
182: push), the local compat symlink, the code fallbacks above, and a README line "formerly opencode-readonly-guard". After the
183: new package exists, one optional step holds the old npm name: publish a stub `opencode-readonly-guard` that depends on
184: the new package and re-exports it, then `npm deprecate` it with a pointer. Without it the old name stays free for anyone;
185: it matters only where instructions that name it survive (history, transcripts). Untested; the maintainer's decision.
186: 
187: **First slice.** If the maintainer decides to rename: one M pull request (step 2 and the shims). If undecided, nothing
188: needs doing: keeping the name is free. **Waits for 2.x:** nothing is blocked, but decide first, so the V2 entry
189: (`Plugin.define({ id, setup })`) is born with the final id and plugin storage, if keyed by id, never splits.
190: 
191: ## 5. Effort, risks, test plan
192: 
193: - Rename PR (script, prose, shims, tests): M. Doctor legacy detection: S. Hosting rename + remote: S (manual, one click).
194:   Local switch and global config: S but the only step that can leave sessions unguarded. Sibling docs: S. Zero-shim variant: S+.
195: - Risks: C fail-open (silent, whole machine); D learned rules and log history look lost; A double load while any old
196:   build stays configured; `rename.ts` is textual (it would also rewrite pinned test literals, hence the registry-key
197:   guard); `prettier` reflows 3 files; a squatter on the old npm name until a stub is published.
198: - Test plan: unit tests for the fallback order (option, new env, old env, new path, old path), the herdr file, doctor with
199:   an old-name entry, a pinned registry-key test (exists: `copies.test.ts:5-6`). Integration: the existing suite after the
200:   rename plus one new case that loads two builds through different specs (reuse `copyPlugin()`), asserting one rule set
201:   as in scenario B. Manual before the first renamed build on the maintainer's machine: `prototype/sidebyside.ts` and
202:   `doctor` from the new folder.
203: - Mechanical proof (scratch copy with its own git root, `tmp/scratch-ap`): `bun run typecheck` exit 0; `bun test test/unit`:
204:   1114 pass, 0 fail; `oxlint --deny-warnings` exit 0; `prettier --check` fails on README, `test/integration/package.test.ts`,
205:   `test/unit/doctor.test.ts` until `--write`. The final script (registry keys kept, 35 files; `tmp/scratch-ap2`, after
206:   `git init` there, as oxlint reads the parent's `.gitignore` otherwise): typecheck 0, lint 0, 1114 unit tests pass
207:   (`evidence/unit-ap2.log`), the same 3 files need `prettier --write`. Integration on the copy (own `dist/`, real opencode; `evidence/integration-scratch.log`): first run 30 pass, 4 fail in
208:   1737 s with the machine at load average 16-27: one failure was mine (I had deleted the copy's `opencode.json`, which
209:   the dogfood test reads), three were 120 s spawn timeouts under load. Re-run of those tests alone with `opencode.json`
210:   restored (`integration-rerun.log`): 6 pass, 0 fail. So the whole suite passes after the rename; no test needed an edit.
211: 
212: ## 6. Questions for the maintainer
213: 
214: 1. Is the move to role-based policy (read-only plus worker and orchestrator roles) decided? If not, keep the name.
215: 2. Descriptive (`opencode-agent-policy`) or evocative (`opencode-clearance`)? Or `@silopolis/<name>`: do you own that scope?
216:    (A scope avoids the global-name race and the similarity rule, at the cost of a longer install line.)
217: 3. Full rename (tools, env, store, command) or partial (package, repo and CLI only; ids stay `readonly_guard_*` for ever)?
218: 4. Shims for 1-2 releases, or zero shims and two manual `mv` commands for your own store and log?
219: 5. Rename the local folder (needs symlink, worktree repair, global config edit) or keep it until the entry is touched anyway?
220: 6. Hold the old npm name with a deprecated stub after the first publish, or accept the squatting risk?
221: 7. New command name (`/policy-review`) or keep the neutral `/guard-review`?

(End of file - total 221 lines)
</content>

    },
    env: { OPENCODE_LOG_LEVEL: "DEBUG" },
    script: {
      scenarios: {
        "SCENARIO:leaks": [
          {
            tools: [
              {
                name: "bash",
                args: {
                  command: "yes 'filler line for the spill file 0123456789' | head -c 70000; printenv [redacted:envvar]",
                  description: "big output, secret at the end",
                },
              },
              { name: "bash", args: { command: "printenv [redacted:envvar]", description: "small" } },
              { name: "task", args: { description: "sub", prompt: "SCENARIO:sub go", subagent_type: "explore" } },
            ],
          },
          { text: `Result: the token is ${fakes.env.[redacted:envvar]} as you can see` },
          { text: "second answer" },
        ],
        "SCENARIO:sub": [{ text: `subagent saw ${fakes.env.[redacted:envvar]}` }],
      },
    },
    // requests without tools: the title generator, and the compaction (its system prompt is about summarizing)
    fallback: (ctx) =>
      /summar/i.test(textOf(ctx.messages[0]?.content))
        ? { text: `## Summary\nThe user token was ${fakes.env.[redacted:envvar]}.` }
        : { text: "Title" },
  }),
})
const rel = (path: string) => relative(l.box.dir, path)
function* filesUnder(dir: string): Generator<string> {
  for (const name of readdirSync(dir)) {
    const path = join(dir, name)
    const info = statSync(path)
    if (info.isDirectory()) yield* filesUnder(path)
    else yield path
  }
}
try {
  const out = await l.serve(async (api) => {
    const sid = await api.session()
    await api.say(sid, "SCENARIO:leaks")
    await api.say(sid, "second turn")
    const callsBefore = l.trace().filter((t) => t.hook === "experimental.chat.messages.transform").length
    const requestsBefore = l.mock.requests().length
    await api.post(`/session/${sid}/summarize`, { providerID: "mock", modelID: "scripted" })
    const messages = await api.messages(sid)
    const eventsBefore = 0
    void eventsBefore
    return { sid, callsBefore, requestsBefore, apiJsonHits: l.count(JSON.stringify(messages)) }
  })
  const exp = await l.run(["export", out.sid], 120_000)
  const trace = l.trace()
  const requests = l.mock.requests()
  const compactionRequests = requests.slice(out.requestsBefore).map((r) => ({
    seq: r.seq,
    hasTools: r.hasTools,
    hits: l.count(JSON.stringify(r.body)),
    messages: r.body.messages.length,
  }))
  const textParts = l
    .parts(out.sid)
    .map((p) => JSON.parse(p.data))
    .filter((d) => d.type === "text")
    .map((d) => ({ hits: l.count(JSON.stringify(d.text)), len: String(d.text).length, summary: /Summary/.test(String(d.text)) }))
  // every file under the sandbox, except the harness's own files, that holds a fake secret
  const skip = new Set(["requests.jsonl", "trace.jsonl", "control.json", "opencode.json", "gh"])
  const onDisk: Record<string, number> = {}
  for (const path of filesUnder(l.box.dir)) {
    if (skip.has(path.split("/").at(-1)!) || path.includes("/.git/") && !path.includes("snapshot")) continue
    let data: Buffer
    try {
      data = readFileSync(path)
    } catch {
      continue
    }
    const n = l.count(data.toString("latin1"))
    if (n) onDisk[rel(path).replace(/rg-sandbox-[A-Za-z0-9]+/, "<sb>").replace(/[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}/g, "<id>")] = n
  }
  const spill = [...filesUnder(l.box.dir)].filter((p) => p.includes("tool-output")).map((p) => ({ file: rel(p).replace(/[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}/g, "<id>"), hits: l.count(readFileSync(p, "latin1")), bytes: statSync(p).size }))
  const bashParts = l
    .parts(out.sid)
    .map((p) => JSON.parse(p.data))
    .filter((d) => d.type === "tool" && d.tool === "bash")
    .map((d) => ({ desc: d.state.input.description, outLen: String(d.state.output).length, outHits: l.count(String(d.state.output)), tail: String(d.state.output).slice(-200).replace(/\n/g, "\\n") }))
  const summary = {
    hooksOn,
    where: l.where(),
    apiJsonHits: out.apiJsonHits,
    textParts,
    bashParts,
    spill,
    transformCalls: { beforeCompaction: out.callsBefore, total: trace.filter((t) => t.hook === "experimental.chat.messages.transform").length },
    textCompleteCalls: trace.filter((t) => t.hook === "experimental.text.complete").map((t) => ({ hit: t.textHit, len: t.textLen })),
    compactingHookFired: trace.some((t) => t.hook === "experimental.session.compacting"),
    compactionRequests,
    exportHits: l.count(exp.stdout),
    exportStatus: exp.status,
    onDisk,
    eventsWithSecret: trace.filter((t) => t.hook === "event" && t.hit).map((t) => `${t.type}:${t.ptype ?? t.field ?? ""}:${t.tool ?? ""}:${t.status ?? ""}`),
  }
  console.log(JSON.stringify(summary, null, 1))
  keepEvidence(l, `05-leakpaths-${hooksOn ? "on" : "off"}`, summary)
} finally {
  assertNoLeaks(l)
}

```

3: Branch `research/redaction`, opencode 1.19.3. Everything below was run against the real opencode with a scripted
4: mock provider (no model, FAKE secrets only). Paths are relative to the worktree; `E:` = `.state/rog-redact/evidence/`,

10: ## 1. Verdict
11: 
12: - An in-plugin redaction layer IS feasible with documented 1.19.3 hooks: nothing real reaches the provider, the
13:   stored rows, the API, `opencode export` or a compaction request when `tool.execute.after`, `chat.message`,
14:   `experimental.chat.messages.transform` and `experimental.text.complete` all redact (E:05-leakpaths-on: 0 hits
15:   everywhere, 8 requests/6 db parts/5 api hits without).
16: - No single hook is enough. `tool.execute.after` does not fire for tool ERRORS or for `!` commands, and its
17:   `output.output` is undefined for MCP tools; `messages.transform` is the net that catches those and old history,
18:   but it does not see the title request and does not change storage.
19: - `shell.env` cannot DELETE (it receives an empty `env`, opencode merges `process.env` afterwards); it can BLANK.
20:   It is a soft barrier: `/proc/$PPID/environ` still holds everything, and the shared allowlist lets `cat` read it.
21: - Detection is value-based first (exact values of secret-NAMED variables, 4-8 ms per MB), shapes second (40-120 ms
22:   per MB), a NAME=value context rule third; transformed secrets (base64, split, reversed) defeat all three.
23: - Recommendation: build the redaction layer as an opt-out module of this plugin, first slice = values+shapes in
24:   `after` + `transform` (with a per-part cache) + `chat.message` + `text.complete` + log redaction; move `env` and
25:   `printenv *` to `ask` meanwhile (they are 5 of 19 secret-printing forms the allowlist lets through).
26: 
27: ## 2. Findings
28: 
29: ### Harness (and how reusable it is)
30: 
31: `P:mock-provider.ts` (scripted SSE provider, 127.0.0.1 port 0, `--script script.json --requests requests.jsonl
32: --port-file`, header documents the JSON format), `P:lib.ts` (sandbox + clean environment + self-check),
33: `P:analysis.ts`, `P:README.md`. Baseline run: `P:exp1-baseline.ts` -> E:01-baseline (secret printed by `bash`: 1 hit in
34: the next provider request, 2 in `part.data` (`state.output` and `state.metadata.output`), 2 in the API).
35: Reuse for the TODO "Deterministic e2e": works as is for `opencode serve` + HTTP API and for `opencode run`;
36: scenario = marker in the first user message, step = number of assistant messages in the request, requests without
37: tools (title generator, compaction) get a fallback; adapter `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` is downloaded once into a
38: shared cache (CI needs a cache or network once). Cost: about 1 s per scripted step (200 steps = 2-5 minutes),
39: dominated by opencode. NOT tested: permission prompts (ask/always replies through the API), streaming reasoning.
40: Gotchas: `withServer()` kills the server after its timeout (a long session needs more); never `spawnSync` opencode
41: from the process that hosts the mock (it blocks the mock).
42: 
43: ### Harness hazards (sandbox() hands the caller's environment to opencode)
44: 
45: Claim: `sandbox()` (`test/helpers.ts`) builds the child environment from `childEnv()`, which removes only `GIT_*` and
46: `HERDR_*`: every credential of the caller goes to the child opencode, its tools and its plugins.
47: Evidence: `P:hazard-sandbox-env.ts` -> E:hazard-sandbox-env.json: 172 caller variables, 168 in the sandbox, 16
48: credential-looking NAMES, 16 of 16 with the caller's value, and the GitHub token is among them. Nothing in the
49: current tests prints an environment, but any test that runs `env`, any opencode log or any `opencode.db` in a
50: sandbox (they live under `/tmp/rg-sandbox-*`) may keep a real token. Fix: a deny pattern on names in `childEnv()`
51: (S, about 15 lines plus a unit test; the e2e tests with `realHome` need an explicit pass-through of the provider key
52: they use, so S-M overall). My harness replaces `box.env` in place with an allowlist and fake secrets.
53: 
54: ### R1 / H1: `tool.execute.after`. Confirmed, with three holes
55: 
56: - Mutating `output.output` changes BOTH the next provider request and the stored `part.state.output` (and so the
57:   API, which reads the same rows): E:02-after-redact, per tool (bash, read, grep, glob, plugin tool, MCP tool, task):
58:   request 0, db output 0, api output 0. Without it: 1/1/1 for each.
59: - Hole 1, metadata: `state.metadata` is stored and served as well: bash `metadata.output` (full copy of the output),
60:   read `metadata.preview`/`loaded` keep the secret (db 1, 2 hits) unless the hook also redacts `output.metadata`
61:   and `output.title` (E:02-after-redact-meta: all 0). The model never gets metadata (request 0 in both variants).
62: - Hole 2, MCP: for MCP tools `output.output` is `undefined`; the result is `output.content[{type,text}]`
63:   (trace shape in E:02-after-observe). A redactor that only touches `output.output` leaves the MCP secret in the
64:   request and the database; walking every string of `output` fixes it (`probe_leak`: 0/0/0).
65: - Hole 3, errors: the hook does NOT fire when the tool fails: `read` of a missing file, a plugin tool that throws,
66:   a command refused by a `tool.execute.before` hook that throws (E:02b-errors-redact: after fired only for the 2 bash
67:   calls that completed). The error text (which echoes paths and, for the write guard, command fragments) is stored
68:   in `state.error` and sent to the model: 3 of 5 results still leaked with `after`+`chat` redacting.
69: - It fires for every tool tried: built-ins (`bash`, `read`, `grep`, `glob`), plugin tools, MCP tools, and `task`
70:   (the subagent's final text is the `task` output and is redacted; the subagent's own `bash` call fires it too).
71:   Not tried: `webfetch`, `edit`, `write`, `todowrite`, `skill`, `question`.
72: - Tool INPUT is stored and re-sent too (`state.input`, the assistant's `tool_calls`): a secret the model typed into
73:   a command (`Authorization: Bearer ...`) stays in the request and the database (E:02b-errors-redact, input hits 3).
74:   `tool.execute.before` could rewrite args, but that changes what runs; `transform` is the place for inputs.
75: - `chat.message` (user text): redacting `output.parts` changes storage and the provider request, the title
76:   request included (E:02b-errors-redact: user text 0 hits; without: also sent to the title generator).
77: - Events: `message.part.updated` for a RUNNING bash part carries the live output (`metadata.output`) and
78:   `message.part.delta` carries assistant text before any hook runs (E:02-after-redact-meta: 4 of 63 events). The
79:   final state is clean; the stream, and old SQLite pages (see R5), are not.
80: Confidence: high (7 tools x 3 variants x 3 places, plus errors). Hook order: before -> shell.env -> after.
81: 
82: ### R2 / H2: `experimental.chat.messages.transform`. Confirmed, with one gap
83: 
84: - Provider request is changed, storage is not: turn 1 with the hook off (secret enters history), hook switched to
85:   redact, turn 2: request 4 (whole history) 0 hits; database 2 hits and API 2 hits unchanged
86:   (E:03-transform-effect). So it also covers history that already holds a secret and is a pure send-time filter.
87: - It covers what `after` misses: with ONLY transform redacting, errors, inputs and the user text are clean in every
88:   request that carries history (E:02b-errors-transform: requests 2 and 3 0 hits, database 12 hits).
89: - Frequency: once per model call that carries history: main loop steps, subagent steps (other session in the same
90:   hook), and the compaction request (E:05-leakpaths-on: 5 calls for 5 requests with history). NOT for the title
91:   generator (request without tools): a user message with a secret reaches the title model unless `chat.message`
92:   redacted it; after a `!printenv` as the first action the title request carried the tool output (E:08-usershell).
93:   The hook input is `{}`: no session id; use `message.info.sessionID`.
94: - Cost, history of 200 assistant steps and ~1 MB of tool output (E:03-transform-cost-*, whole session of 201 calls):
95:   values only 3.5 s in the hook (median 17 ms, max 44); values+shapes+context on every string every call 164 s
96:   (median 895 ms, max 1.75 s): too slow; the same with a per-part "clean" cache (key = part id, state, size) 13 s
97:   (median 50 ms, max 227 ms). The cost is per string, not per byte (one 1 MB string takes 70-100 ms, R6). Wall time of
98:   a run varies 117-301 s with opencode's own load and is not comparable. Redaction must be deterministic (same
99:   replacement every turn) so the provider's prompt prefix stays stable.
100: Confidence: high for effect/frequency, medium for cost (one machine, noisy).
101: 
102: ### R3 / H3: `shell.env`. Blank yes, delete no, soft barrier
103: 
104: - The hook receives `output.env = {}` (0 keys, only `cwd`, `sessionID`, `callID`): opencode merges `process.env`
105:   after it. Deleting does nothing (E:04-shellenv "delete": everything still printable). Blanking sets the name to the
106:   empty string: `printenv X` prints an empty line, `${X-unset}` prints empty (set but empty), `env | cut -d=` still
107:   lists the NAME. Works in the bash tool, in subagents, in `opencode run` (E:04b-run, E:04-shellenv) and in the `!`
108:   command (POST /session/:id/shell: the hook fires with a callID, no command known).
109: - It is a soft barrier. `tr '\0' '\n' < /proc/$PPID/environ | grep -c '^[redacted:envvar]='` gives 1 in every variant
110:   (opencode's own environment block), and `cat /proc/$PPID/environ` is `allow` under the shared rules
111:   (E:check-paths.txt). Deleting from `process.env` inside the plugin (`delete process.env.X`) makes the children's
112:   variable truly unset but `/proc/$PPID/environ` still lists it (E:04c-scrub). Only a launcher that starts opencode
113:   without the secrets (outside the plugin) is a real barrier.
114: - Per command: the `tool.execute.before` hook runs first for the same callID, so a plugin can remember the command
115:   and decide in `shell.env`. Giving `gh` its token and nothing else works (fake `gh` reports "authenticated" only with
116:   the token): a naive `^gh ` match also hands the token to `gh auth status; printenv [redacted:envvar] | wc -c` (it printed 41
117:   chars); a strict "exactly one simple command, no `;|&$()` or backtick" match did not (E:04-shellenv
118:   "blank+gh-naive" / "blank+gh-strict"). The repo's tokenizer (`src/shell.ts`) can decide that. `gh auth token`
119:   prints the token anyway (it asks today); output redaction is the second layer. `!` commands have no known command
120:   (nothing runs `tool.execute.before` for them): they get only the default environment.
121: - `git push`/`mise` need credentials the same way: give them per command or use a credential helper that reads a
122:   file the role cannot `cat` (not tested; the agent shares the uid).
123: Confidence: high.
124: 
125: ### R4: `experimental.text.complete`. Works for stored text and the next request
126: 
127: Assistant text that echoes a secret (main agent, subagent final text, compaction summary) is redacted: stored text
128: 0 hits, next request 0 hits (E:05-leakpaths-on: the hook fired 4 times, 3 with a hit; summary part 0 hits).
129: The live `message.part.delta` events still carry the raw text. Not tested: reasoning parts.
130: 
131: ### R5: other leak paths (all hooks on, `P:exp5-leakpaths.ts`; E:05-leakpaths-on / -off)
132: 
133: | Path | Covered by | Evidence |
134: | --- | --- | --- |
135: | provider request, `part.data`, API, `opencode export` | after + transform + chat + text | on: 0/0/0/0; off: 8/6/5/5 |
136: | compaction request | transform (runs for it) | on 0 hits, off 3 |
137: | compaction summary | `text.complete` | stored summary 0 hits (off 1) |
138: | tool-output spill file (`xdg/data/opencode/tool-output/tool_*`) | NOT covered: the file is raw (70041 bytes, 1 hit); rereading it by `read`/`cat` is covered | on |
139: | opencode logs at DEBUG | nothing to cover: no hit in any log file in either run | partly verified |
140: | event stream (running bash output, text deltas) | NOT covered | on: `message.part.updated` (bash running), `message.part.delta` |
141: | SQLite file and WAL | NOT covered: old row versions (running parts, deltas) stay: db file 1 hit, WAL 5 after redaction | on |
142: | `!` command output | only transform (no before/after hook runs) | E:08-usershell: db 2 hits, request 2 carried it |
143: | title generator | only `chat.message` for user text | E:08-usershell request 1 |
144: | plugin `events.jsonl` (commands, `asked` patterns) | a wrapper around `write()` | `P:exp7-eventlog.ts`: 3 hits -> 0 |
145: | files in the project (snapshot repository) | out of scope | not tested |
146: The bash tool keeps the TAIL of a long output and writes the whole to the spill file; hooks see the tail only.
147: 
148: ### R6: detection (`P:bench-detect.ts`, E:06-detection.json, `P:redactor.js`)
149: 
150: - Corpus: 1 MB of this repository (sources, rules, tests, lockfile hashes, typings). Median of 7 runs, ms per MB, ordinary
151:   text / text with 21 inserted secrets: values by `split` (8 values) 7.6 / 21.8; values by one regex alternation 3.7 / 7.5;
152:   shapes (15 regexes) 41 / 123; context rule 13 / 11; all three 67 / 88. A literal-prefix prefilter was not faster (56 / 106).
153: - Recall (what survives): values alone catch only the secrets the process holds (all 8 fake env values, none of the
154:   others); shapes alone miss unprefixed values (AWS secret key, DB password, JWT signing secret) and everything
155:   with a lookalike-free format; the context rule catches `NAME=value`, `"client_secret": "..."` and `oauth_token: ...`
156:   (as in `hosts.yml`) of other hosts; all three together catch everything except a bare unknown 40-character string.
157: - Transformations defeat all of it (`P:evasion.ts`, E:evasion.json): base64, base64url, hex, reversed, split over
158:   two lines, spaced characters, rot13, the last 20 characters and `${T:0:12}` survive; plain, JSON-escaped and the
159:   first 30 characters are caught. A hash is no longer a secret.
160: - False positives on the 1 MB corpus: shapes 0, values 0, context 2 (TypeScript annotations `credential: CredentialOAuth`;
161:   tune by requiring a digit or 16 characters). Value policy on the maintainer's real environment (COUNTS only): 16
162:   secret-NAMED variables, 12 kept, 4 skipped (3 paths, 1 number), shortest kept value 24 characters. A synthetic
163:   tricky environment (`SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `AUTH_MODE=oauth`, `TOKEN_TTL=3600`, `COOKIE_SECURE=true`, `API_KEY_FILE=/...`)
164:   keeps only `[redacted:envvar]` and `PASSWORD_PROMPT=changeme`. Policy used: name pattern
165:   `TOKEN|SECRET|PASSWORD|[redacted:envvar]|[redacted:envvar]|[redacted:envvar]|CREDENTIAL|AUTH|COOKIE|DSN|KEY$`; skip values shorter than 8, numbers,
166:   words, paths and URLs without credentials; longest value first.
167: - Replacement format: `[redacted:[redacted:envvar]]` for values (the NAME is not a secret and tells the model what it was),
168:   `[redacted:github]` for shapes, `[redacted:value]` for the context rule. Keep it deterministic.
169: Confidence: high for speed and recall on this corpus, medium for false positives (one corpus).
170: 
171: ### R7: scope, rtk, the write guard, and `env` / `printenv`
172: 
173: - Scope: the leak is a property of the session, not of a role: value needles come from one `process.env`, cost is
174:   tiny, so default ON for all agents, opt out by option (`redact: false` or `agents.exclude`). Credential injection
175:   (`shell.env` per command) is the role-dependent part. The write guard only needs the plugin's hook plumbing and
176:   `copy.active()` checks; it shares nothing else.
177: - Plugin order (`P:exp6-order.ts`, E:07-order-*): hooks of several plugins run in the order of the `plugin` list, for
178:   every hook, and the second plugin sees what the first changed (a rewritten command, a redacted output). So list the
179:   redacting plugin LAST for `after` (it sees what others produced), and note that a command rewriter listed before the
180:   write guard shows it the rewritten command (`rtk ls`), listed after, the original. rtk itself was not run or read.
181: - `rtk env` (cleared environment, fakes only, E:rtk-env.txt) filters, it does not redact: `[redacted:envvar]=...` and an AWS
182:   secret key are printed in full, an unclassified `[redacted:envvar]` is dropped. `rtk env`/`rtk env -f TOKEN` ask under the
183:   shared rules, `rtk read ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` is allowed. Whether the rtk plugin rewrites `env` was not verified.
184: - `env` and `printenv *`: the shared rules let 20 of 28 secret-related command forms run without a prompt, 19 of them
185:   print secret material (E:check-paths.txt): `env`, `printenv`, `printenv NAME`, `env | grep GIT`, `echo $TOKEN`,
186:   `echo "$TOKEN"`, `printf '%s' "$TOKEN"`, `cat /proc/self/environ`, `cat /proc/$PPID/environ`, `tr ... < /proc/$PPID/environ`,
187:   `strings`/`od -c`/`rg -a` on it, `cat /proc/*/environ`, `cat ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `git config --list`,
188:   `git config --get-regexp .`, `echo ${!GITH*}`. Only `declare -p`, `export -p`, `ps e`, `ps auxe` block; `xargs -0`,
189:   `gh auth token`, `set`, `compgen -v` ask. Moving `env` and `printenv *` to ask closes 5 of the 19.
190:   With the redaction layer on, all 19 print `[redacted:NAME]` for secrets the process holds. Recommendation: move
191:   `env`/`printenv *` to ask now (S, with cases), say in the README that it is not a boundary, and keep the
192:   `/proc` and `echo $VAR` forms for the redaction layer; once value redaction ships and is on by default, put
193:   `env`/`printenv` back (their output shows `NAME=[redacted:NAME]`). Residual after that: a secret in a variable with
194:   a harmless name and no known shape, a secret not in the environment of opencode, and transformed secrets.
195: 
196: ## 3. Not verified, and why
197: 
198: - opencode 2.x hooks and the lower bound 1.18.29 (only 1.19.3 installed); `experimental.*` hooks may change.
199: - Real providers: reasoning/thinking parts (stored, `text.complete` untested for them), provider-side caching and logging.
200: - The TUI (what the user sees while streaming), the real rtk plugin and its config (private), `webfetch`/`edit`/`write`
201:   results, permission prompt flows with the mock, a model that transforms a secret on purpose.
202: - Terminal output of `opencode run` with redaction on (it prints tool output live on stderr).
203: - Opencode's behaviour when `process.env` is scrubbed at startup for providers that read keys lazily.
204: - Prompt-cache impact of redaction (requires a real provider).
205: 
206: ## 4. Recommendation
207: 
208: Design: a `redact` module in this plugin (`src/redact.ts`), default on, with these parts, in this order of value:
209: 1. `tool.execute.after`: redact `output.output`, `output.title`, `output.metadata`, and every string of an MCP
210:    result (`output.content`). 2. `chat.message`: redact the user's text before it is stored (also protects the title
211: request). 3. `experimental.chat.messages.transform`: values + shapes over every part, with a per-part clean cache;
212: catches errors, inputs, `!` commands, old history and compaction. 4. `experimental.text.complete`. 5. Redact every
213: event before `events.jsonl` is written. 6. Optional, separate switch: `shell.env` blank for secret-named variables
214: and a strict per-command token for `gh`/`git push`/`mise` (decided by the analyzer; unknown commands get none).
215: Collect values once at startup from `process.env` (never log them), name-based policy above, minimum length 8.
216: Smallest useful first slice: items 1 to 4 with values only plus the shape table, no `shell.env`, behind
217: `redact: true` default; ship the `env`/`printenv` change first.
218: Cannot be fixed in a plugin: spill files, SQLite pages, the event stream, `/proc/$PPID/environ` (launcher), the title
219: request for `!` output, transformed secrets. Waits for 2.x (unverified): a real output/permission hook model, and
220: storage hooks that would let the plugin keep raw data out of the database.
221: 
222: ## 5. Effort, risks, test plan
223: 
224: - PR1 `src/redact.ts` + unit tests (fake secrets, shapes table, evasion list, false-positive corpus): M.
225: - PR2 hooks in `plugin.ts` + options + `copy.active()` on each hook + `events.jsonl` wrapper + docs: M.
226: - PR3 `shell.env` blanking / per-command credential: S-M (needs the maintainer's decision, see below).
227: - PR4 `test/` mock provider + harness + integration tests for redaction (request, database, API): M; the same mock
228:   serves the TODO "Deterministic e2e".
229: - PR5 `childEnv()` name denylist in `test/helpers.ts`: S. PR6 `env`/`printenv *` to ask + cases: S.
230: - Risks: `experimental.*` API drift (the integration suite must run on each opencode bump, like the copies test);
231:   redaction changes what the model reads (fixture strings shaped like tokens, 2 context false positives per MB of
232:   TypeScript); non-deterministic replacement breaks prompt caching; every new hook needs the multi-copy check;
233:   per-string cost without the cache (0.9 s per call at 1 MB of history).
234: - Test plan: unit (policy, longest-first, boundaries, no secret in any message of a thrown error or log); integration
235:   with the mock provider asserting `requests.jsonl`, `part.data` and `GET /session/:id/message` for: each tool kind,
236:   tool error, MCP, subagent, `!` command, compaction, export, two plugins in order, `opencode run`; a canary
237:   credential variable in the test runner to prove the self-check; time budget test on 1 MB.
238: 
239: ## 6. Questions for the maintainer
240: 
241: 1. Move `env` and `printenv *` to `ask` now, as an interim, knowing it closes 5 of 19 paths? Or wait for redaction?
242: 2. Redaction on by default for every agent, or opt-in? (It changes what tools return.)
243: 3. Is a soft `shell.env` barrier (blank) wanted, or only redaction? And do you want `gh`/`git push`/`mise` tokens
244:    injected per command by the plugin, or moved out of the environment (credential helper, launcher)?
245: 4. Same package, or a separate redaction plugin (the name says "readonly")? It fits the rename discussion.
246: 5. Is "not covered: spill files, SQLite WAL, event stream, title request" acceptable, or is a launcher-level fix
247:    (opencode started without secrets) the real answer for the worker fleet?
248: 6. The harness hazard fix (PR5) and the mock provider PR (PR4): independent PRs, in this order?

<skill_content name="opencode-session-migrate">
# Skill: opencode-session-migrate

# OpenCode Session Migration

This skill allows you to migrate project and session metadata in the OpenCode database when a project's filesystem path changes.

## Workflow

1. **Identify Paths**
   - Determine the **old path** (the original directory where the project was located).
   - Determine the **new path** (the current absolute path of the project directory).

2. **Update Project Worktree**
   Update the `project` table to reflect the new location.
   ```bash
   sqlite3 ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db "UPDATE project SET worktree = '[new-path]' WHERE worktree = '[old-path]';"
   ```

3. **Update Session Directories**
   Update all sessions associated with that project to point to the new directory.
   ```bash
   sqlite3 ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db "UPDATE session SET directory = '[new-path]' WHERE project_id = (SELECT id FROM project WHERE worktree = '[new-path]');"
   ```

## Verification
After migration, the user can verify the change by listing sessions or attempting to resume a session from the new directory.

- Run `/sessions` to ensure the project is recognized.
- Use `/resume <session-id>` to verify the context loads correctly from the new path.

Base directory for this skill: ~/.agents/skills/opencode-session-migrate
Relative paths in this skill (e.g., scripts/, reference/) are relative to this base directory.
Note: file list is sampled.

<skill_files>

</skill_files>
</skill_content>

## Your open questions

### D3: shell.env, credentials, and what redaction can't cover

**shell.env blank (D3b).** Before each bash command, the plugin would set secret-named variables to an empty string for that one command.
- **Gain:** `env`, `printenv X` and `echo $X` print nothing, even when redaction misses something.
- **Cost:** every command that needs a credential from the environment breaks (`gh`, git push over HTTPS, mise downloads, npm). The variable's name stays visible.
- **Bypass:** `/proc/$PPID/environ` still holds opencode's real environment. D4(b) blocks the literal path, but a renamed path or an interpreter still reads it.
- **Verdict:** it only slows a leak down. It's useful only if credentials are given back to the commands that need them.

**Credentials (D3c) can be handled three ways:**
1. **The plugin injects them per command.** Every variable is blanked, and the token goes back only to a command that is exactly one `gh …`, with no `; | & $()`. The strict match worked in the tests; a naive one leaked. The token still sits in opencode's own environment, and the plugin becomes a credential broker where a parser bug means a leak.
2. **Move them out of the environment.** Agents start without `[redacted:envvar]` at all. `gh` keeps its own login, either in the keyring or in `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`. git uses `gh` as credential helper (`gh auth setup-git`), and mise reads its own config.
   - Nothing remains in `env` or `/proc/*/environ` to leak.
   - What's left: a plaintext `hosts.yml`, which D4(b) blocks and the keyring avoids, and `gh auth token`, which must stay ask or block.
   - This lives in dotfiles/cem (the env file, a launcher), not in the plugin.
3. **A launcher for agent sessions only.** `launch-worker.sh` or herdr starts opencode with `env -u [redacted:envvar] …`. Same effect for agents, and your interactive shells stay unchanged.

My recommendation is 2 or 3, without injection; then nothing needs blanking. The pending token rotation is the natural moment: put the new token in gh's keyring instead of the env file.

**What redaction can't cover (D3d):**

| Path | What happens | Reaches the provider? |
|---|---|---|
| Spill file | A long output (70 KB in the test) is cut: the redacted tail stays in the chat, the full raw text goes to `~/.local/share/opencode/tool-output/` | No. Reading the file back is redacted. Local disk. |
| SQLite pages and WAL | A part is written while it runs, before the hook redacts it; the old bytes stay until a checkpoint or VACUUM | No, and not in the API or export either. Local disk. |
| Event stream | Live output and streaming text reach the TUI before any hook runs | No. Your screen. |
| Title after a `!` command | If a session starts with `!cmd`, its raw output goes to the small model that writes the title | Yes, rarely |
| `/proc/$PPID/environ` | opencode's own environment | Yes if printed. Fixed by D3c 2 or 3 plus D4(b). |
| Transformed secrets (base64, split, reversed) | Not recognisable | Yes. It needs an agent that encodes on purpose, which is outside the accident model. |

My recommendation: accept them and document them under "What it does not do", with optional pruning of spill files.

### D5: what each tool does, and where it goes (`[redacted:repo]/oap/`)

| Tool | What it does | Future |
|---|---|---|
| `watch` | Polls the worker panes and answers "Allow once" when the shared rules allow the command; stops on anything else | Polling moves to `oap/`. Its approval logic is replaced by `oap check --role` (WP6b). |
| `stages.mjs` | Splits a command line into pipeline stages for `watch` | Replaced by the roles engine, then dropped |
| `lib-once.sh`, `once` | Press "Allow once" only after checking the highlighted option on screen (a blind Enter once opened "Always allow") | `oap/` |
| `peek` | Shows a worker's status and its pending prompt | `oap/` |
| `launch-worker.sh` | Worktree, herdr workspace, install, inputs, start opencode, send the brief (verify and resend) | `oap/`, with paths turned into variables |
| `retire-worker.sh` | Refuses a dirty or unpushed tree, harvests `.state/<name>`, removes the worktree and workspace | `oap/` |
| `make-brief.sh` | Header plus task file gives a brief | `oap/`, with the brief templates |
| `deploy-main.sh` | Rebuilds the main checkout's `dist/`: scratch build and tests, spot checks, swap, rollback, `doctor` | `oap/` (could become a mise task later) |
| `export-sessions.sh` | Fleet exporter, then redactor, then local scrub, then `--check` | `oap/` (worth a signal to istc and nvim, whose tools it chains) |
| `box.sh` | Sandbox with its own git root for opencode probes | `oap/` (mostly superseded by `sandbox()`) |
| `tally.mjs` | Tallies the commands that still ask, with before/after tables for allowlist PRs | `oap/` (a candidate `oap review` subcommand) |

- `.state/rog-orch/` keeps the state file, journal and notes.
- The move happens during the local switch (WP3c), since the paths change then anyway.
- chezmoi-orch owns the store, so it needs to agree first. I'll send it a signal asking.

# darse

> Le darse de Silopolis: the basin where vessels are laid down and refitted.
> Part of the Silopolis workshop: libre, open, portable information systems.

darse is L1 in the Silopolis ecosystem (`amiraute:spec/drs/DR-001-four_layer_ecosystem_model.md`): the project factory.
It ships scaffolding templates, toolchain pins, quality gates and CI adapters that any project can be laid down from, and later refitted with (`radoub`, Phase B), via Copier.

## What lives here

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `spec/`, `spec/drs/`, `spec/contracts/` | darse's own decision records and contracts, indexed per-directory (`DR-021`); entry point `spec/README.md` |
| `project/milestones/`, `project/tasks/` | darse's own milestone and task records (`DR-017`/`DR-018`/`DR-021` branch, milestone and index model); entry point `project/roadmap.md` |
| `project/TODO.md`, `project/roadmap.md` | darse's own piloting files: day-to-day kanban and structural sequencing (`DR-021`) |
| `docs/` | darse's own documentation site, Diataxis-structured, Quarto-published (`DR-020`); `mise run docs:build` |
| `copier.yml` | the Copier entrypoint, at this repo's own root (`CT-001.R01`/`R05`, `_subdirectory: template`): what makes this repo a git-tracked Copier template a consumer can `copier copy` *and* `
| `template/` | the Copier template source, addressed via `_subdirectory`: `core`/`runtime`/`quality` module fragments (`template/copier/`) with real content, shared includes (`template/includes/`) (`
| `tests/` | the update round-trip harness (`mise run test:roundtrip`, `CT-003.R01`-`R04`/`R05` plus two doctrine checks), asserted against a real, throwaway-tagged Copier round trip of the whole repo

What does **not** live here: domain content, lab material, or anything specific to a generated project.
Domain flavor enters only through optional template modules, never base assumptions (`DR-005`).

# Trusted publishing for npm packages

Table of contents

-   [How trusted publishing works](#how-trusted-publishing-works)
-   [Supported CI/CD providers](#supported-cicd-providers)
-   [Configuring trusted publishing](#configuring-trusted-publishing)
-   [Managing dist-tags with trusted publishing](#managing-dist-tags-with-trusted-publishing)
-   [Learn more](#learn-more)

Trusted publishing allows you to publish npm packages directly from your CI/CD workflows using [OpenID Connect (OIDC)](https://openid.net/developers/how-connect-works/) authentication, eliminating the need for long-lived npm tokens. This feature implements the [trusted publishers industry standard](https://repos.openssf.org/trusted-publishers-for-all-package-repositories) specified by the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), joining a growing ecosystem including [PyPI](https://docs.pypi.org/trusted-publishers/), [RubyGems](https://guides.rubygems.org/trusted-publishing/), and other major package registries in offering this security enhancement.

**Note:** Trusted publishing requires [npm CLI](/cli/v11) version 11.5.1 or later and Node version 22.14.0 or higher.

## [How trusted publishing works](#how-trusted-publishing-works)

Trusted publishing creates a trust relationship between npm and your CI/CD provider using OIDC. When you configure a trusted publisher for your package, npm will accept publishes from the specific workflow you've authorized, in addition to traditional authentication methods like npm tokens and manual publishes. The npm CLI automatically detects OIDC environments and uses them for authentication before falling back to traditional tokens.

This approach eliminates the security risks associated with long-lived write tokens, which can be compromised, accidentally exposed in logs, or require manual rotation. Instead, each publish uses short-lived, cryptographically-signed tokens that are specific to your workflow and cannot be extracted or reused.

## [Supported CI/CD providers](#supported-cicd-providers)

Trusted publishing currently supports:

-   [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/features/actions) (GitHub-hosted runners)
-   [GitLab CI/CD Pipelines](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/) (GitLab.com shared runners)
-   [CircleCI](https://circleci.com/) (CircleCI cloud)

Self-hosted runners are not currently supported but are planned for future releases.

## [Configuring trusted publishing](#configuring-trusted-publishing)

Trusted publisher setup:Multiple trusted publishersSingle trusted publisher

## [Step 1: Add a first trusted publisher on npmjs.com](#step-1-add-a-first-trusted-publisher-on-npmjscom)

Navigate to your package settings on [npmjs.com](https://www.npmjs.com) and find the "**Trusted Publisher**" section. Under "**Select your publisher**", choose your CI/CD provider by clicking the GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, or CircleCI button.

![Screenshot showing the Trusted Publisher section with Select your publisher label and provider buttons](/packages-and-modules/securing-your-code/trusted-publisher.jpg)

### [For GitHub Actions](#for-github-actions)

Configure the following fields:

-   **Organization or user** (required): Your GitHub username or organization name
-   **Repository** (required): Your repository name
-   **Workflow filename** (required): The filename of your workflow (e.g., `publish.yml`)
    -   Enter only the filename, not the full path
    -   Must include the `.yml` or `.yaml` extension
    -   The workflow file must exist in `.github/workflows/` in your repository
-   **Environment name** (optional): If using [GitHub environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/using-environments-for-deployment) for deployment protection
-   **Allowed actions** (optional): `npm stage publish` is always allowed. Choose whether this trusted publisher can also publish directly with `npm publish` or [manage dist-tags](#managing-dist-tags-with-trusted-publishing) with `npm dist-tag`. These permissions are independent. See [Staged publishing for npm packages](/staged-publishing) for more information on staged publishing.

![Screenshot of GitHub Actions multiple trusted publisher configuration form](/packages-and-modules/securing-your-code/multiple-trusted-publisher-github-actions.jpg)

### [For GitLab CI/CD](#for-gitlab-cicd)

Configure the following fields:

-   **Namespace** (required): Your GitLab username or group name
-   **Project name** (required): Your project name
-   **Top-level CI file path** (required): The path to your CI file (e.g., `.gitlab-ci.yml`)
    -   Must include the `.yml` extension
-   **Environment name** (optional): If using [GitLab environments](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/environments/)
-   **Allowed actions** (optional): `npm stage publish` is always allowed. Choose whether this trusted publisher can also publish directly with `npm publish` or [manage dist-tags](#managing-dist-tags-with-trusted-publishing) with `npm dist-tag`. These permissions are independent.

![Screenshot of GitLab CI/CD multiple trusted publisher configuration form](/packages-and-modules/securing-your-code/multiple-trusted-publisher-gitlab.jpg)

### [For CircleCI](#for-circleci)

Configure the following fields:

-   **Organization ID** (required): Your CircleCI organization ID (UUID format). You may find it from your CircleCI Organization Settings Overview page.
-   **Project ID** (required): Your CircleCI project ID (UUID format). You may find it from your CircleCI Project Settings Overview page.
-   **Pipeline definition ID** (required): The pipeline definition ID (UUID format). You may find it from your CircleCI Project Settings under Project Setup page.
-   **VCS origin** (required): The VCS origin URL for your project (e.g., `github.com/myorg/myrepo`)
-   **Context IDs** (optional): Restrict publishing to jobs using specific CircleCI contexts. You may find them from your CircleCI Organization Settings Contexts.
-   **Allowed actions** (optional): `npm stage publish` is always allowed. Choose whether this trusted publisher can also publish directly with `npm publish` or [manage dist-tags](#managing-dist-tags-with-trusted-publishing) with `npm dist-tag`. These permissions are independent.

For more in-depth information see [CircleCI's guide](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/deploy/deploy-to-npm-registry/).

![Screenshot of CircleCI multiple trusted publisher configuration form](/packages-and-modules/securing-your-code/multiple-trusted-publisher-circleci.png)

**Note:** Each package can have up to 10 trusted publishers configured at the same time, so you can publish from different CI/CD providers or workflows for the same package.

**Note:** Trusted publisher configurations created before May 20, 2026 are automatically set to allow `npm publish` only — no behavior change occurs for current workflows. Configurations created before Sep 03, 2026 require you to explicitly select at least one allowed action — no behavior change occurs for current workflows. Configurations created after Sep 03, 2026 are automatically set to allow `npm stage publish`, and you can choose whether to also permit direct publishing with `npm publish`.

## [Step 2: Configure your CI/CD workflow](#step-2-configure-your-cicd-workflow)

### [GitHub Actions configuration](#github-actions-configuration)

Add the required OIDC permissions to your workflow. Here's a complete example:

name: Publish Package

on:

  push:

    tags:

      \- 'v\*'

permissions:

  id-token: write  \# Required for OIDC

  contents: read

jobs:

  publish:

    runs-on: ubuntu\-latest

    steps:

      \- uses: actions/checkout@v6

      \- uses: actions/setup\-node@v6

        with:

          node-version: '24'

          registry-url: 'https://registry.npmjs.org'

          package-manager-cache: false  \# never use caching in release builds

      \- run: npm ci

      \- run: npm run build \-\-if\-present

      \- run: npm test

      \- run: npm publish  \# Or: npm stage publish

The critical requirement is the `id-token: write` permission, which allows GitHub Actions to generate OIDC tokens. Learn more in [GitHub's OIDC documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect).

### [GitLab CI/CD configuration](#gitlab-cicd-configuration)

Configure the OIDC ID token in your pipeline:

stages:

  \- test

  \- build

  \- publish

variables:

  NODE\_VERSION: '24'

test:

  stage: test

  image: node:${NODE\_VERSION}

  script:

    \- npm ci

    \- npm test

publish:

  stage: publish

  image: node:${NODE\_VERSION}

  id\_tokens:

    NPM\_ID\_TOKEN:

      aud: "npm:registry.npmjs.org"

    SIGSTORE\_ID\_TOKEN:

      aud: sigstore

  script:

    \- npm ci

    \- npm run build \-\-if\-present

    \- npm publish  \# Or: npm stage publish

  only:

    \- tags

The `id_tokens` configuration tells GitLab to generate an OIDC token for npm. Learn more in [GitLab's OIDC documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/cloud_services/).

**Note:** Don't forget to configure id\_tokens 'aud' to `"npm:registry.npmjs.org"` in your GitLab pipeline.

### [CircleCI configuration](#circleci-configuration)

Set the `[redacted:envvar]` environment variable with an OIDC token from CircleCI, and npm CLI handles the token exchange automatically. Here's a complete example:

version: 2.1

jobs:

  publish:

    docker:

      \- image: cimg/node:22.14

    steps:

      \- checkout

      \- run:

          name: Install dependencies

          command: npm ci

      \- run:

          name: Run tests

          command: npm test

      \- run:

          name: Build

          command: npm run build \-\-if\-present

      \- run:

          name: Publish to npm with OIDC

          command: |

            export NPM\_ID\_TOKEN=$(circleci run oidc get --claims '{"aud": "npm:registry.npmjs.org"}')

            npm publish  # Or: npm stage publish

workflows:

  publish:

    jobs:

      \- publish:

          filters:

            tags:

              only: /^v.\*/

            branches:

              ignore: /.\*/

The `circleci run oidc get` command retrieves an OIDC token from CircleCI. When `[redacted:envvar]` is set, the npm CLI automatically exchanges it for a short-lived publish token. Learn more in [CircleCI's OIDC documentation](https://circleci.com/docs/openid-connect-tokens/).

## [Managing trusted publisher configurations](#managing-trusted-publisher-configurations)

You can add or remove your trusted publisher configurations at any time through your package settings on [npmjs.com](https://npmjs.com) → Packages → YOUR\_PACKAGE → Settings → Trusted publishing. Each package can have up to 10 trusted publisher connections at the same time, and each connection can be added or deleted independently as needed. To add another provider (for example, publishing from both GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD), click the Add trusted publisher button and select the provider.

![Screenshot of the Add trusted publisher button for configuring multiple trusted publishers](/packages-and-modules/securing-your-code/add-trusted-publisher.png)

**Note:** Existing trusted publisher connections cannot be changed. The provider and required fields for a connection are fixed once it's created. To change them, delete the connection and create a new one.

## [Trusted publisher configuration expiry](#trusted-publisher-configuration-expiry)

A newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within 2 days. The first successful publish validates the configuration and binds it to the repository's immutable identity.

If the configuration is not validated within 2 days, it expires and can no longer be used or edited. To continue using trusted publishing, delete the expired configuration, create a new one, and complete the first publish within 2 days.

## [Recommended: Restrict token access when using trusted publishers](#recommended-restrict-token-access-when-using-trusted-publishers)

Once you've configured trusted publishers for your package, we strongly recommend restricting traditional token-based publishing access for enhanced security.

## [How to configure maximum security](#how-to-configure-maximum-security)

1.  After enabling trusted publishers, navigate to your package's **Settings** → **Publishing access**
2.  Select **"Require two-factor authentication and disallow tokens"**
3.  Save your changes by clicking on **Update Package Settings**

## [Why this matters](#why-this-matters)

Trusted publishers use short-lived, scoped credentials that are generated on-demand during your CI/CD workflow, eliminating the need for long-lived tokens. By restricting traditional token access while using trusted publishers, you reduce potential security risks associated with credential management.

For even stronger security, configure your trusted publisher with **stage-only permissions** (allow `npm stage publish` but not `npm publish`). This ensures all CI-automated publishes go through the [staged publishing](/staged-publishing) flow, requiring a maintainer to review and approve each package with 2FA via the CLI or [npmjs.com](https://www.npmjs.com) before it becomes publicly available. Combined with disallowing tokens, this provides the maximum security posture for your packages.

**Note:** The "disallow tokens" setting only affects traditional token authentication. Your trusted publishers will continue to work normally, as they use OIDC tokens.

## [Migration tip](#migration-tip)

If you're transitioning from token-based publishing:

1.  Set up trusted publishers first and verify they work
2.  Then restrict token access as described above
3.  [Revoke any existing automation tokens](/revoking-access-tokens) that are no longer needed

This ensures a smooth transition without disrupting your release process.

## [Automatic provenance generation](#automatic-provenance-generation)

When you publish using trusted publishing from GitHub Actions or GitLab CI/CD, npm automatically generates and publishes [provenance attestations](/generating-provenance-statements) for your package. This happens by default—you don't need to add the `--provenance` flag to your publish command.

**Note:** Provenance generation is not currently supported for CircleCI. Packages published via CircleCI trusted publishing will not include provenance attestations.

![Screenshot showing provenance badge/information on a package page](/packages-and-modules/securing-your-code/trusted-publisher-provenance.png)

Provenance provides cryptographic proof of where and how your package was built, allowing users to verify its authenticity. This automatic generation only applies when all of these conditions are met:

-   Publishing via trusted publishing (OIDC)
-   Publishing from a public repository
-   Publishing a public package

**Note:** Provenance generation is [not supported for private repositories](https://github.blog/changelog/2023-07-25-publishing-with-npm-provenance-from-private-source-repositories-is-no-longer-supported/), even when publishing public packages.

## [Disabling provenance generation](#disabling-provenance-generation)

While we strongly recommend keeping provenance enabled, you can disable it if needed. Set the `provenance` option to `false` in any of these ways:

**Using environment variable:**

NPM\_CONFIG\_PROVENANCE\=false npm publish

**In your `.npmrc` file:**

provenance=false

**In your `package.json`:**

{

  "publishConfig": {

    "provenance": false

  }

}

## [Security best practices](#security-best-practices)

## [Prefer trusted publishing over tokens](#prefer-trusted-publishing-over-tokens)

When trusted publishing is available for your workflow, always prefer it over long-lived tokens. Traditional npm tokens pose several security risks:

-   They can be accidentally exposed in CI logs or configuration files
-   They require manual rotation and management
-   If compromised, they provide persistent access until revoked
-   They often have broader permissions than necessary

Trusted publishing eliminates these risks by using short-lived, workflow-specific credentials that are automatically managed and cannot be extracted.

## [Handling private dependencies](#handling-private-dependencies)

While trusted publishing handles the publish operation, you may still need authentication for installing private npm dependencies. For this scenario, we recommend:

\# GitHub Actions example

\- uses: actions/setup\-node@v6

  with:

    node-version: '24'

    registry-url: 'https://registry.npmjs.org'

    package-manager-cache: false  \# never use caching in release builds

\# Use a read-only token for installing dependencies

\- run: npm ci

  env:

    NODE\_AUTH\_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM\_READ\_TOKEN }}

\# Publish uses OIDC - no token needed

\- run: npm publish

Always use [read-only granular access tokens](/creating-and-viewing-access-tokens#creating-granular-access-tokens-on-the-website) for installing dependencies. This limits potential damage if the token is ever compromised.

## [Additional security measures](#additional-security-measures)

Consider implementing these additional security practices:

-   Use [deployment environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/using-environments-for-deployment) to add approval requirements
-   Enable [tag protection rules](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/managing-repository-settings/configuring-tag-protection-rules) to control who can create release tags
-   Regularly audit your trusted publisher configurations
-   Remove any unused publish tokens from your npm account

## [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

If you encounter an "Unable to authenticate" (ENEEDAUTH) error when publishing, first verify that the workflow filename matches exactly what you configured on [npmjs.com](https://npmjs.com), including the `.yml` extension. All fields are case-sensitive and must be exact. Also ensure you're using GitHub-hosted runners, GitLab.com shared runners, or CircleCI cloud, as self-hosted runners are not currently supported. For GitHub Actions specifically, check that the `id-token: write` permission is set in your workflow. For CircleCI, verify that your Organization ID, Project ID, and Pipeline definition ID match your CircleCI configuration.

**Note:** npm does not verify your trusted publisher configuration when you save it. Double-check that your repository, workflow filename, and other details are correct, as errors will only appear when you attempt to publish.

To publish from GitHub, your package's `repository.url` field in `package.json` must exactly match your GitHub repository. This may be an issue for misconfigured packages, but could also impact publication from forks that haven't updated `package.json` to match the forked repo.

If your package has private dependencies and `npm install` or `npm ci` is failing with authentication errors, remember that trusted publishing is not intended for `npm install`. You'll still need to provide a read-only token for installing private packages as shown in the examples above.

For packages in private repositories, provenance will not be generated even though you're using trusted publishing. This is a [known limitation](https://github.blog/changelog/2023-07-25-publishing-with-npm-provenance-from-private-source-repositories-is-no-longer-supported/) that applies regardless of whether your package itself is public or private.

Some GitHub Actions workflows use `workflow_call` to invoke other workflows that run `npm publish`, or use `workflow_dispatch` for manual publishing. When this happens, validation checks the calling workflow's name instead of the workflow that actually contains the publish command, which can cause configuration mismatches. The `id-token: write` permission must also be given to both parent and child workflows.

## [Limitations and future improvements](#limitations-and-future-improvements)

Trusted publishing currently supports only cloud-hosted runners. Support for self-hosted runners is intended for a future release. Each package can have up to 10 trusted publishers configured at the same time. Existing trusted publisher connections cannot be changed. To change them, delete the connection and create a new one.

## [Managing dist-tags with trusted publishing](#managing-dist-tags-with-trusted-publishing)

**Note:** dist-tags with OIDC Trusted publishing requires npm CLI version 11.21.0 (or later) and 12.2.0 (or later).

To allow a workflow to manage your package's [distribution tags](/adding-dist-tags-to-packages), select **Allow npm dist-tag** for its trusted publisher configuration in your package settings. This option is disabled by default.

Dist-tag access is independent of direct publishing. You can allow a configuration to stage packages and manage dist-tags without allowing `npm publish`. Enabling or disabling it on one configuration does not change the permissions of other configurations.

After configuring trusted publishing for your package and CI/CD workflow, run `npm dist-tag` commands directly in that workflow. The npm CLI authenticates automatically using your CI/CD provider's OIDC identity.

For example, list the tags, point `next` to version `2.1.0`, and check the result:

npm dist-tag ls example-package

npm dist-tag add example-package@2.1.0 next

npm dist-tag ls example-package

To remove a tag, run `npm dist-tag rm example-package beta` in the same workflow. Reading a private package's tags with trusted publishing also requires dist-tag permission; public tags remain readable without authentication.

If a tag operation reports that the trusted publisher cannot manage dist-tags, ask a package maintainer to enable **Allow npm dist-tag** for the configuration used by your workflow. Permission to publish or stage a package does not grant this access automatically.

OIDC authentication supports `npm publish`, `npm stage publish`, and the dist-tag operations described above. Other stage subcommands (`npm stage list`, `npm stage view`, `npm stage approve`, `npm stage reject`) require interactive authentication and cannot use OIDC tokens, as these actions require proof of presence and can only be performed via the CLI or [npmjs.com](https://www.npmjs.com). Other npm commands such as `install`, `view`, or `access` still require traditional authentication methods. The `npm whoami` command is not a check of trusted publishing permissions; verify them using the operation you intend to perform.

We intend to expand trusted publishing support to additional CI/CD providers and enhance the feature based on community feedback.

**D3c, still yours: the two options turned out closer than they looked.**

- **gh and git need none either.** `env -u [redacted:envvar] gh auth status` shows a valid keyring login, and git already uses `gh auth git-credential` as its helper.
- **Option 3 would be a dotfiles change.** herdr marks its panes with `HERDR_ENV=1`, but `herdr agent start` can't run a custom command. That leaves an `opencode` shell function in the dotfiles that starts opencode without secret-named variables. It would break only scripts or skills that call those services with an env key (unknown: chezmoi-orch can list what uses each variable).
- **For the GitHub token,** "rotation" can become "revoke the leaked token and delete the line". No new token is needed, unless something like mise's GitHub rate limits needs it. That needs checking.

**npm how-to for the release task (T-009), checked against npm's docs today:**
1. **Account:** sign up on npmjs.com, taking the username `silopolis` if it's free, which gives you `@silopolis` at no cost. Turn on 2FA for login and writes.
2. **First publish:**
   - It has to use a token, because trusted publishing is set up in the package's own settings, and the package doesn't exist yet.
   - Create a granular token (read-write, all packages, 1 to 7 days) and store it as a repo secret.
   - Push tag `v0.2.0`, and `release.yml` publishes with `id-token: write` so v0.2.0 gets provenance.
   - A local `npm publish` would fail, because `publishConfig.provenance` is true.
3. **Then:** go to the package's Settings, then Trusted publishing, and pick GitHub Actions, `silopolis`, `opencode-agent-policy`, `release.yml`. It must publish successfully within 2 days.
4. **Lock down:** under Publishing access, choose "Require 2FA and disallow tokens", then revoke the token and delete the secret.
5. **Requirements:**
   - npm ≥11.5.1 and Node ≥22.14 (mise pins 24.22.1).
   - `repository.url` must match the renamed repo exactly.
   - You chose not to hold the old name, so there's nothing to do there.

## The finding
- **The value is inherited, not re-read.** The herdr server and kitty both hold `[redacted:envvar]`, and so does every process from there down to my shell.
- **Nothing unsets it.** `010-env_user.sh` only sources `~/.config/env` and never runs `unset`, so deleting the line stops the file from setting it but doesn't remove it from processes that already have it.
- **New panes inherit it.** Every new herdr pane and kitty window gets the old value from its parent until herdr and kitty restart. That restart would close every orchestrator's panes.
- **After revocation, `gh` breaks in all of them.** `gh` prefers the variable over its keyring login, so it would fail with a 401 in every new pane too, wave 1 workers included.

**The fix is one dotfiles line**, after the `source` in `010-env_user.sh`: `unset [redacted:envvar]`. Every new shell then drops the inherited value without restarting herdr. That's chezmoi-orch's change to make.

## Answer to chezmoi-orch's question: revoke now, don't wait for me
- **The token has been exposed since 2026-11-03.**

  - My only tool that calls `gh` is `retire-worker.sh`, and it gets the same prefix until then.
- **The other orchestrators and your editors** will get 401s from `gh` until they're restarted or use `env -u`. chezmoi-orch won't restart them, so that's your call.

Note: This command is unaware of workspaces.
Prerequisites
Before using npm trust commands, ensure the following requirements are met:

npm version: npm@11.15.0 or above is required. Use npm install -g npm@^11.15.0 to update if needed.
Write permissions on the package: You must have write access to the package you're configuring.
2FA enabled on account: Two-factor authentication must be enabled at the account level. Even if it's not currently enabled, you must enable it to use trust commands.
Supported authentication methods: Granular Access Tokens (GAT) with the bypass 2FA option are not supported. Legacy basic auth (username and password) credentials will not work for trust commands or endpoints.
Package must exist: The package you're configuring must already exist on the npm registry.

Description
Configure trust relationships between npm packages and CI/CD providers using OpenID Connect (OIDC). This is the command-line equivalent of managing trusted publisher configurations on the npm website.
For a comprehensive overview of trusted publishing, see the npm trusted publishers documentation.
The [package] argument specifies the package name. If omitted, npm will use the name from the package.json in the current directory.
Each trust relationship has its own set of configuration options and flags based on the OIDC claims provided by that provider. OIDC claims come from the CI/CD provider and include information such as repository name, workflow file, or environment. Since each provider's claims differ, the available flags and configuration keys are not universal—npm matches the claims supported by each provider's OIDC configuration. For specific details on which claims and flags are supported for a given provider, use npm trust <provider> --help.
Permissions
When creating a trust relationship, you must specify at least one permission flag to indicate which operations the trusted publisher is allowed to perform:

--allow-publish: Allows the trusted publisher to run npm publish for the package.
--allow-stage-publish: Allows the trusted publisher to run npm stage for the package. The alias --allow-staged-publish is also accepted.

At least one of these flags is required when creating a trust configuration. You can specify both to grant both permissions.
Provider Options
The required options depend on the CI/CD provider you're configuring. Detailed information about each option is available in the managing trusted publisher configurations section of the npm documentation. If a provider is repository-based and the option is not provided, npm will use the repository.url field from your package.json, if available.
Currently, the registry only supports one configuration per package. If you attempt to create a new trust relationship when one already exists, it will result in an error. To replace an existing configuration:

Use npm trust list [package] to view the ID of the existing trusted publisher
Use npm trust revoke --id <id> [package] to remove the existing configuration
Then create your new trust relationship

Bulk Usage
For maintainers managing a large number of packages, you can configure trusted publishing in bulk using bash scripting. Create a loop that iterates through package names and their corresponding configuration details, executing the npm trust <provider> command with the --yes flag for each package.
The first request will require two-factor authentication. During two-factor authentication, you'll see an option on the npm website to skip two-factor authentication for the next 5 minutes. Enabling this option will allow subsequent npm trust <provider> commands to proceed without two-factor authentication, streamlining the bulk configuration process.
We recommend adding a 2-second sleep between each call to avoid rate limiting. With this approach, you can configure approximately 80 packages within the 5-minute two-factor authentication skip window.

  "content": "---\nid: T-015\ntitle: \"Roles engine, role data and cases\"\nstatus: draft\nmilestone: M-003\ndepends_on: [T-014]\nsize: M-L\nwave: 3\nexecutor: \"build worker, one PR\"\npublish: yes\ncreated: 2026-11-16\nupdated: 2026-11-16\n---\n\n# T-015: Roles engine, role data and cases\n\n## Goal\nOne pull request, `feat(roles): a role engine that decides allow, ask or block for a command line`: `src/roles.ts`, role data under `rules/`, the ratified cases run in the unit suite.\nNo plugin change, no CLI yet (T-016).\n\n## Context digest (research report `inputs/report-roles.md`; prototype `inputs/roles.ts`, `inputs/run-cases.ts`, `inputs/cases-roles.json`)\n- Roles: read-only, worker, orchestrator, deployer, reviewer. A role is a set of capabilities from a reviewed catalogue (data in the repository), never free patterns. Capability matrix in\n  the report, section 2a. Trust model: roles are trusted but fallible; this prevents accidents, it is not a sandbox (an interpreter runs arbitrary code; symlinks are not followed).\n- What the code needs that the analyzer does not have today: a working directory (it does not track `cd`: `parseShell` flattens a line into ordered simple commands), write-target scope\n  (worktree, scratch, own state directory), the own-branch push rule (exact branch, never force, never delete), merge and `gh` write verbs, herdr control scope, script pins by content hash.\n- Measured on the 116 cases: globs alone 65 right with 27 unsafe allows; globs plus code that only blocks 112 right with 4 unsafe allows (all \"this script and no other\"); the strict rule\n  (code turns an ask into a block where a glob allows) 0 unsafe; code deciding (2.x semantics) 116. The prototype was tuned on the corpus: treat 116/116 as a fit.\n- Facts about opencode 1.19.3 that bound the design (report section 2c, evidence files): `tool.execute.before` receives only the tool, session and call ids plus the arguments (bash:\n  `command`, `description`, `workdir`); in a linked worktree opened as the project, `directory`, `worktree` and `project.worktree` are all the linked worktree; opencode's own\n  `external_directory` check refuses `touch`, `rm`, `cp`, `mv`, `mkdir`, `chmod`, `cd` with literal operands and the write tool, but NOT `>`, `tee`, `sed -i`, `ln`, `truncate`,\n  `install`, `dd of=`, `curl -o`, `tar`, `git init DIR`, `find -exec`, `xargs`, `eval`, `bash -c`, interpreters, variables, `$(...)`, and mis-resolves `cd` chains.\n\n## Binding decisions\n- Invariant: a role can only NARROW what the safety check (`src/classify.ts`) accepts; any user pattern in a role goes through `classifyPattern`; a read-only agent's write guard is never\n  switched off by a role. The package ships NO grants (verdict engine first): the engine answers, the coordinator or the project's configuration enforces.\n- Data: `rules/roles.json` (catalogue and role definitions) with a JSON Schema in `rules/schema/`, validated like the other rule files (`test/unit/rules.test.ts`); the ratified cases in\n  `rules/cases-roles.json`, run by a unit test (one case = one assertion, failure message names the case).\n- Unknown means guarded: an unparseable line, an unresolved variable, an `eval`, a pin whose content hash differs: block (or ask where the corpus says ask).\n- Every block message names the allowed alternative (an over-blocked unattended worker stalls).\n- Property test: the strict 1.x decider never allows what the engine blocks or asks.\n- Performance: the prototype took a fraction of a millisecond per decision; assert a loose bound.\n\n## Read first\n`AGENTS.md`, `src/analyze.ts`, `src/shell.ts`, `src/decide.ts`, `src/classify.ts`, `src/rules.ts`, `inputs/report-roles.md` (all), `inputs/roles.ts`, `inputs/run-cases.ts`,\n`inputs/cases-roles.json` (ratified version from T-014).\n\n## Plan\nSTAGE 0: read, PLAN (max 20 lines: module split, how cwd is tracked through `cd`, data format, order of commits, open questions), wait for the go. Then test-first by case groups,\n`mise run check`, push, PR, `READY: <url>`.\n\n## Definition of Done\nAll ratified cases pass; the strict-mode property test passes; schema tests pass; `mise run check` passes; the PR is open.\n\n## Out of scope\nCLI, plugin enforcement, `watch` integration (T-016, T-017), the 2.x hook.\n\n## Changelog\n- 2026-11-16: created (WP6a).\n"
}
